Boil in well-salted water 3 to 4 minutes. Meanwhile brown the butter with the sage until nutty. Lift the pasta into the pan with a slotted spoon, add a splash of pasta water, toss, and finish with cheese and pine nuts.
recipes.cooksNote: Drain the ricotta overnight in a sieve. Undrained ricotta makes a wet filling that soaks through the pasta while it waits on the tray.

recipes.title: Saint-Félicien (Baked, with Walnuts and Honey)
recipes.description: Saint-Félicien is a soft cow's milk cheese from the Rhône, richer and runnier than its cousin Saint-Marcellin. You don't make it at home. What you do is heat it gently until it turns into a sauce, which takes about twenty minutes and feels like cheating.

items: 1 Saint-Félicien, about 180 g, in its terracotta or wooden container
1 small garlic clove, sliced into slivers
A few slices of dry-cured ham

method: Take the cheese out of the fridge an hour ahead. Cold cheese heats unevenly.
Heat the oven to 180°C. Toast the walnuts on a tray for 6 minutes, then roughly chop.
Score a shallow cross in the top rind of the cheese and slip the garlic slivers into the cuts.
Sit the cheese in a small oven dish, tuck the thyme around it, and bake 15 to 18 minutes until the centre is molten and the top is puffed.
While it bakes, toast thick slices of bread.
Take the cheese out, spoon the honey over the top, and scatter the walnuts.
Crack over black pepper and serve straight away with the bread and ham. It sets as it cools, so eat fast.
recipes.cooksNote: If your cheese came in cardboard, move it to a small ceramic dish first. Cardboard scorches.

recipes.title: Châteaubriand
recipes.description: A thick cut from the head of the tenderloin, roasted whole and carved for two. The classic sauce is béarnaise, and I've given you a proper one.

items: 500 g centre-cut beef tenderloin, tied into an even cylinder
1 tbsp tarragon stalks, plus 2 tbsp chopped leaves

method: Salt the beef generously and leave it at room temperature for 45 minutes.
Reduce the vinegar, wine, shallots, and tarragon stalks in a small pan until about 2 tbsp of liquid remain. Strain and cool slightly.
Whisk the yolks with the reduction over a pan of barely simmering water until thick and ribbony, about 4 minutes. The bowl should be warm, never hot.
Off the heat, dribble in the clarified butter while whisking constantly. Season with lemon, salt, cayenne, and the chopped tarragon. Keep it somewhere warm but not hot.
Sear the beef in oil in a heavy pan over high heat, turning every 45 seconds until browned all over, about 6 minutes.
Add the butter, garlic, and thyme, and baste for 3 minutes, tilting the pan and spooning the foaming butter over the top.
Transfer to a 200°C oven for 8 to 10 minutes, until the centre reads 52°C for medium rare. Rest 10 minutes, then carve thick slices across the grain.
recipes.cooksNote: If the béarnaise splits, whisk a fresh yolk with a teaspoon of water in a clean bowl and slowly beat the broken sauce into it. Works nearly every time.

recipes.title: Poulet Rôti
recipes.description: Roast chicken. Every French cook has an opinion about it. Mine: dry brine the day before, start breast side down, and don't stuff it with anything that will slow the cooking.
method: The day before, pat the chicken completely dry, rub the salt all over including under the breast skin, and leave uncovered on a rack in the fridge. The skin dries out, which is what makes it crisp.
Take it out an hour before cooking. Heat the oven to 220°C.
Push the butter under the breast skin and smooth it flat with your fingers. Put the lemon, half the garlic, thyme, and bay inside the cavity. Truss the legs.
Sit the chicken breast side down on the potatoes and shallots in a roasting tin. Roast 25 minutes.
Turn it breast side up, drop the oven to 190°C, and roast another 40 minutes, basting twice with the fat in the tin.
It's done when the thigh joint reads 74°C and the juices run clear. Move it to a board and rest 20 minutes, breast side down for the first 10.
Skim the fat from the tin, deglaze over a burner with the wine, scrape up the sticky bits, and simmer 3 minutes into a thin jus. Carve, pour, serve.
recipes.cooksNote: Resting for 20 minutes sounds excessive and isn't. A chicken carved straight from the oven loses its juice onto the board.

recipes.title: Pommes Anna
recipes.description: Sliced potatoes, butter, salt. That's the entire ingredient list. It bakes into a golden cake with distinct layers, and the only difficult part is patience with the arranging.
method: Heat the oven to 200°C. Slice the potatoes 2 mm thick on a mandoline.
Do not rinse them. The surface starch is the glue that holds the cake together.
Brush a 22 cm ovenproof skillet heavily with clarified butter. Arrange the best slices in a tight overlapping spiral on the base, since this becomes the top when you turn it out.
Build up in layers, brushing each with butter and seasoning lightly. Press down as you go.
Set the pan on the hob over medium heat for 5 minutes until you hear it sizzling and the edges colour.
Cover with foil, bake 30 minutes, then uncover and bake 20 minutes more until the top is deep brown and a knife slides through with no resistance.
Rest 5 minutes, run a knife around the edge, and invert onto a plate in one confident movement.
recipes.cooksNote: Clarified butter matters here. Regular butter has milk solids that burn over the long bake and leave a bitter edge.

recipes.title: Croissant
recipes.description: A two-day project. The dough is laminated with a butter block, folded three times, and each fold traps more layers. Cold dough and cold butter, always.

items: 1 egg, beaten with a splash of milk

method: Mix the détrempe ingredients into a shaggy dough, knead 5 minutes until it comes together, then flatten into a rectangle, wrap, and chill overnight.
Next day, pound the cold butter between two sheets of paper into a 20 cm square. It should bend without cracking, around 14°C.
Roll the dough to 40 by 20 cm, place the butter on one half, fold over, and seal the edges.
Roll out to about 60 by 20 cm, fold in thirds like a letter, wrap, and chill 45 minutes. Repeat twice more, always rolling in the same direction and always chilling between folds.
Roll the finished dough to 40 by 30 cm, 4 mm thick. Cut long triangles with a 10 cm base. Notch the base, stretch slightly, and roll from base to tip.
Set on lined trays, cover loosely, and prove at 24 to 26°C for 2 to 3 hours until visibly puffy and jiggly. Warmer than that and the butter leaks out.
Brush with egg wash and bake at 200°C for 8 minutes, then 180°C for 10 to 12 minutes until deep brown all over. Cool on a rack.
recipes.cooksNote: If butter leaks in the oven, the dough got too warm during folding or the prove was too hot. Both are fixable next time. The croissants will still taste good.

recipes.title: Crème Brûlée
recipes.description: Baked custard with a shattered sugar lid. The custard should barely hold, wobbling in the middle when you shake the ramekin.

items: 6 tbsp demerara or caster sugar, for the top

method: Heat the cream with the vanilla pod and seeds until it steams. Take it off the heat and let it sit 20 minutes to infuse.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar and salt just until combined. Don't beat air into them.
Pour the warm cream over the yolks in a slow stream, whisking. Strain into a jug and skim off any foam.
Divide between six shallow ramekins and set them in a deep tray. Pour hot water halfway up the sides.
Bake at 150°C for 30 to 40 minutes. The edges should be set and the centres still loose.
Cool, then chill at least 4 hours or overnight.
Blot the surface dry, sprinkle an even thin layer of sugar, and blowtorch until it bubbles and turns amber. Wait 2 minutes for it to harden before serving.
recipes.cooksNote: Shallow ramekins beat deep ones. You get a better ratio of caramel to custard, and they bake more evenly.

recipes.title: Pain de Campagne
recipes.description: Country bread with a little rye and a natural starter. Long fermentation does the flavour work while you're asleep.
method: Mix the flours with 350 ml of the water and leave 45 minutes. This rest hydrates the flour and shortens kneading later.
Add the starter and squeeze it through the dough. Rest 30 minutes, then add the salt with the remaining 25 ml water and work it in.
Over the next 3 to 4 hours, do four sets of stretch and folds, spaced 45 minutes apart. The dough should get smoother and airier each time.
When it's risen by about 50 percent and feels alive, tip it out, shape it into a loose round, and rest 20 minutes.
Shape tightly into a boule, seam side up in a floured banneton, and refrigerate overnight, 12 to 16 hours.
Heat a Dutch oven at 250°C for 45 minutes. Turn the loaf out, score once decisively about 1 cm deep, and lower it in.
Bake covered 20 minutes, then uncovered at 220°C for 25 minutes until dark brown. Cool completely on a rack before cutting.
recipes.cooksNote: Cutting bread hot is a real temptation and it ruins the crumb. Give it two hours.

recipes.title: Filet de Bœuf en Croûte
recipes.description: Beef fillet in pastry with a mushroom duxelles. Wellington by another name. The enemy is moisture, so every stage is about drying things out.

items: 12 thin slices prosciutto or Bayonne ham
1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tbsp cream
700 g mushrooms, chestnut or a mix
60 g flour, 1 egg, 150 ml milk, pinch of salt

method: Blitz the mushrooms, shallots, and garlic to a coarse paste. Fry in butter over medium-high for 20 to 25 minutes until every drop of water has gone and it looks dark and dry. This takes longer than you expect.
Add the Madeira and thyme and cook until dry again. Season and cool completely.
Sear the salted fillet in a very hot pan for 90 seconds a side, all around. Cool, then brush with mustard.
Make two thin crêpes if using. Lay cling film on the bench, overlap the ham slices into a sheet, spread the duxelles over, add the crêpe, then the beef.
Roll it up tightly using the cling film, twist the ends like a sweet wrapper, and chill 30 minutes until firm.
Roll the pastry out to 4 mm. Unwrap the beef, sit it on the pastry, and wrap, trimming the overlap and sealing the seam underneath. Chill another 30 minutes.
Egg wash, score the top lightly, and bake at 210°C for 25 to 30 minutes until the internal temperature is 50°C. Rest 15 minutes before slicing thickly.
recipes.cooksNote: A soggy bottom comes from steam. The crêpe layer absorbs it, and so does baking on a preheated tray.

recipes.title: Steak au Poivre
recipes.description: Steak under a crust of cracked pepper with a cream and cognac sauce. Crush the peppercorns yourself, coarsely. Pre-ground pepper turns to dust and burns.

items: 2 sirloin or fillet steaks, 250 g each, 3 cm thick
3 tbsp black peppercorns, coarsely cracked and sieved of dust

method: Take the steaks out of the fridge 40 minutes early. Salt them well.
Press the cracked pepper firmly onto both flat sides. Press, don't sprinkle.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan until it just begins to smoke. Lay the steaks in and don't move them for 3 minutes.
Flip, add half the butter, and cook 3 minutes more for medium rare, basting. Move to a plate to rest.
Lower the heat, add the shallots to the pan, and soften 2 minutes.
Take the pan off the flame, add the cognac, and return it to the heat. It may flame briefly. Let it reduce almost to nothing.
Add the stock, reduce by half, then the cream and mustard. Simmer until it coats a spoon, whisk in the remaining butter, and pour over the rested steaks along with any juices from the plate.
recipes.cooksNote: Sieve the cracked pepper. The fine dust burns in the pan and makes the sauce bitter, while the coarse pieces give you that crunch.

recipes.title: Magret de Canard
recipes.description: Duck breast from a fattened bird, cooked from a cold pan so the fat renders slowly. Served pink, with something sharp alongside.
method: Score the skin in a diamond pattern, cutting through the fat but not into the meat. Season heavily with salt.
Lay the breasts skin side down in a cold, dry pan. Turn the heat to medium-low.
Let them render for 12 to 15 minutes. Pour off the fat two or three times as it collects, and save it for potatoes. The skin should end up thin, flat, and deep gold.
Flip and cook 3 minutes on the flesh side. Move to a board and rest 10 minutes, skin side up.
Pour off all but a spoonful of fat. Soften the shallots, then add the wine and reduce to a syrup.
Add the stock, honey, vinegar, and fruit. Simmer until it thickens.
Off the heat, swirl in the cold butter. Slice the duck thinly across the grain, pour the sauce around rather than over, and serve.
recipes.cooksNote: Starting in a cold pan feels wrong and is correct. A hot pan seizes the skin before the fat underneath can melt out.

recipes.title: Baguette
recipes.description: Four ingredients, and one of the harder things in this book. The flavour comes from a poolish left overnight.
method: Whisk the poolish ingredients, cover, and leave at room temperature 12 to 16 hours. It's ready when domed and just starting to fall in the centre.
Mix the poolish with the remaining flour, water, and yeast. Rest 30 minutes, then add the salt and knead 6 minutes until smooth.
Bulk ferment 2 hours, folding the dough over itself every 40 minutes.
Divide into three, pre-shape into loose logs, and rest 20 minutes under a cloth.
Shape each into a 35 cm baguette: flatten gently, fold the top third down, the bottom third up, seal along the seam with the heel of your hand, then roll to length.
Prove seam side up in a floured couche for 60 to 75 minutes.

Flip onto a peel, slash at a shallow angle with 4 or 5 overlapping cuts, and bake at 250°C with plenty of steam for 12 minutes, then 230°C without steam for 10 minutes until dark gold and crackling as it cools.
recipes.cooksNote: For steam at home, put a metal tray on the oven floor while preheating and throw a cup of boiling water into it as the bread goes in. Stand back.

recipes.title: Gratin Dauphinois
recipes.description: Sliced potatoes baked in cream and milk with garlic. No cheese in the traditional version, though nobody will stop you. The starch thickens the cream, which is why you don't rinse the slices.

items: 1.4 kg floury potatoes, peeled and sliced 3 mm
2 garlic cloves, one halved and one crushed

method: Rub a wide gratin dish with the cut garlic clove, then butter it well.
Put the milk, cream, crushed garlic, plenty of salt, pepper, and a good grating of nutmeg into a wide pan.
Add the potato slices and bring to a bare simmer. Cook 8 minutes, stirring gently so nothing sticks. The liquid will thicken noticeably.
Tip everything into the dish and level the top, pressing the potatoes down so the liquid comes almost to the surface.
Bake at 160°C for 60 to 75 minutes. Low and slow is right here.
It's done when the top is browned in patches and a knife meets no resistance.
Rest 15 minutes before serving. It sets slightly and cuts far better.
recipes.cooksNote: Floury potatoes, not waxy. You want them to give up starch and half-collapse into the cream.

recipes.title: Canapés au Saumon Fumé
recipes.description: Smoked salmon on something crisp with something creamy. Simple, so the details are all you have: good salmon, cold butter, sharp knife.

items: 12 slices dense rye or pain de mie
2 tbsp finely chopped dill, plus sprigs
½ red onion, sliced paper thin

method: Beat the crème fraîche, cream cheese, chopped dill, horseradish, lemon zest, and a squeeze of juice until smooth. Season and chill.
Cut the crusts off the bread and slice each piece into two rectangles or rounds.
Brush lightly with olive oil and bake at 180°C for 8 to 10 minutes until crisp at the edges but not brittle. Cool.
Soak the onion slices in cold water with a splash of lemon for 10 minutes, then drain. This takes the raw bite out.
Pipe or spoon the cream onto each base.
Drape a folded ribbon of salmon on top. Folding gives height and looks better than lying it flat.
Finish with capers, onion, a dill sprig, black pepper, and a tiny squeeze of lemon just before serving.
recipes.cooksNote: Assemble within an hour of serving. The bases go soft after that and there's no rescuing them.

recipes.title: Soupe à l'Oignon Gratinée
recipes.description: Onions cooked down for the better part of an hour, beef stock, bread, and a lid of melted cheese. The colour of the onions determines everything.

items: 1.2 kg onions, halved and sliced thin

method: Melt the butter with the oil in a wide heavy pot. Add the onions and a good pinch of salt, cover, and sweat 15 minutes.
Uncover, add the sugar, and cook over medium heat for 45 minutes, stirring every few minutes. They'll go from pale to gold to deep mahogany. If they stick, add a splash of water and scrape.
Stir in the flour and cook 2 minutes.
Add the wine, scraping the base, and reduce by half.
Pour in the stock with the herbs. Simmer 30 minutes, then season and add the brandy.
Toast the baguette slices until dry. Ladle the soup into ovenproof bowls, float the bread on top, and heap the cheese over so it covers the rim.
Grill until the cheese is bubbling and browned in patches. Let it sit 2 minutes so nobody burns their mouth.
recipes.cooksNote: The 45 minutes of caramelising is the recipe. There's no shortcut, and pale onions give you a thin, sweet soup with no depth.

recipes.title: Sole Meunière
recipes.description: Flour, butter, lemon, parsley. Four steps and one pan. It's the dish that made Julia Child change careers, and it takes about eight minutes.

items: 2 whole Dover sole, 400 g each, skinned and trimmed, or 4 fillets
2 tbsp clarified butter or oil, for frying
1 lemon, half juiced, half cut into wedges

method: Pat the fish bone dry. Season both sides.
Season the flour and dredge the fish, pressing lightly, then shake off every bit of loose flour. Excess flour burns and clouds the butter.
Heat the clarified butter in a large pan over medium-high until shimmering.
Lay the fish in, presentation side down. Cook 4 minutes without touching it.
Turn carefully with two spatulas and cook 3 minutes more. Slide onto warm plates.
Wipe the pan, add the cold butter, and swirl over medium heat until it foams and the solids turn nut brown and smell like toffee. Roughly 90 seconds.
Take it off the heat immediately, add the lemon juice (it will spit), stir in the parsley, and pour over the fish. Serve with lemon wedges and boiled potatoes.
recipes.cooksNote: Beurre noisette goes from perfect to burnt in about ten seconds. Have your lemon juice measured and standing by before you start browning.

recipes.title: Otoro Nigiri Sushi
recipes.description: Fatty tuna belly over seasoned rice. There's nowhere to hide with this one, so buy the best fish you can and handle it as little as possible.

items: 250 g otoro (tuna belly), sushi grade, well chilled
Wasabi, real if you can get it
Tezu: 200 ml water mixed with 1 tbsp rice vinegar

method: Wash the rice in several changes of water until it runs mostly clear, then drain in a sieve for 20 minutes.
Cook with the water and kombu. Remove the kombu just before it boils. Rest 10 minutes off the heat, lid on.
Warm the vinegar, sugar, and salt until dissolved. Don't boil it.

Turn the rice into a wide bowl, pour the vinegar mix over a spatula so it spreads, and cut through the rice with slicing motions while fanning it. You want it glossy and at body temperature, never cold.
Trim the otoro, removing sinew. Slice against the grain at a slight angle into pieces about 8 cm by 3 cm, roughly 5 mm thick.
Wet your hands with tezu. Take about 18 g of rice and squeeze it lightly into an oval. Light pressure. It should hold together but collapse in the mouth.
Smear a little wasabi on the fish, lay the rice on top, then flip and shape with two fingers. Serve fish side down onto the plate.
recipes.cooksNote: Keep the tuna in the fridge until the moment you slice it, and use your longest, sharpest knife in a single pulling stroke. Sawing tears the fat.

recipes.title: Yokohama Style Ramen
recipes.description: Iekei ramen: pork bone and chicken broth with a heavy soy tare, thick straight noodles, spinach, and nori. It sits somewhere between tonkotsu and Tokyo shoyu, and it's rich enough that a small bowl goes a long way.

items: 1 onion, 1 leek, 6 garlic cloves, 5 cm ginger
800 g pork belly, rolled and tied
200 ml soy, 100 ml mirin, 100 ml sake, 50 g sugar, water to cover
Blanched spinach, sheets of nori, spring onion, chopped garlic, sesame oil, marinated soft eggs

method: Blanch the bones in boiling water for 10 minutes, drain, and scrub off the scum. This step decides whether your broth is clean or muddy.

Cover with the 5 litres of fresh water, add the aromatics, and boil hard for 5 to 6 hours, topping up water as it drops. A rolling boil emulsifies the fat, which is what makes the broth opaque and creamy.
Braise the pork belly in the chashu liquid at a low simmer for 2 hours. Cool it in the liquid, then chill before slicing.
Warm all the tare ingredients to 70°C, hold 20 minutes, then strain. Don't boil it.
Strain the broth. Season a test bowl with about 3 tbsp tare per 350 ml broth and adjust.
Boil the noodles hard for the time on the packet, usually 90 seconds to 2 minutes. Drain thoroughly.
Tare into the bowl, hot broth over it, noodles, then chashu, spinach, egg, nori standing up at the side, spring onion, and a small pile of raw chopped garlic.
recipes.cooksNote: Six hours is a weekend project. A pressure cooker gets you 80 percent of the way in 90 minutes at high pressure.

recipes.title: Kare (Japanese Curry)
recipes.description: Sweeter, thicker, and gentler than its Indian ancestor. Most Japanese homes use a block of curry roux from a box, which is genuinely good, but making the roux yourself takes fifteen minutes and tastes noticeably better.

items: 600 g beef chuck or chicken thigh, cubed

method: Brown the meat hard in oil, in batches. Set aside.
Cook the onions in the same pot over medium-low heat for 20 minutes until deeply golden and sweet. This is the flavour base, so don't cut it short.
Add the garlic, ginger, and grated apple. Cook 2 minutes.
Return the meat, add stock, soy, tomato paste, and honey. Simmer 40 minutes.
Meanwhile melt the butter in a small pan, whisk in the flour, and cook over low heat for 10 minutes until it smells nutty and turns light brown. Stir in the spices off the heat.
Add the carrots and potatoes to the pot, simmer 15 minutes until just tender.

Whisk a ladle of hot broth into the roux, then stir the loosened roux into the pot. Simmer 10 minutes more until it's thick enough to hold a line when you drag a spoon through it. Serve over rice with pickled ginger.
recipes.cooksNote: It's better the next day, no question. The starch keeps thickening overnight, so add a splash of water when reheating.

recipes.title: Chicken Karaage
recipes.description: Marinated fried chicken with a potato starch coating. Double frying is the difference between good and very good.

items: 800 g boneless chicken thigh, skin on, in 4 cm pieces
120 g potato starch, plus more for dusting

method: Mix the chicken with soy, sake, mirin, ginger, garlic, and sesame oil. Marinate 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to overnight in the fridge.
Beat in the egg, then work in enough potato starch to make a loose batter clinging to each piece.
Roll each piece in dry potato starch just before frying and shake off the excess.
Heat oil to 160°C. Fry in batches for 3 minutes. The chicken should be pale gold and just cooked.
Rest on a rack for 4 minutes. The residual heat finishes the inside.
Raise the oil to 190°C and fry again for 60 to 90 seconds until deep golden and audibly crunchy.
Drain on a rack, salt lightly, and serve with lemon and mayo.
recipes.cooksNote: Potato starch, not cornstarch. Cornstarch gives a denser, sandier crust that softens quickly.

recipes.title: Kare Udon
recipes.description: Leftover curry thinned with dashi and poured over thick udon. It's a weeknight dish built for the day after curry night.

items: 400 g fresh or frozen udon noodles
300 ml Japanese curry (from recipe 3, or 3 blocks of roux)
150 g thinly sliced pork belly or beef
1 tbsp potato starch mixed with 2 tbsp water

method: Simmer the onion in the dashi for 5 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the sliced pork, separating the pieces as they go in, and cook 3 minutes.
Stir in the curry, soy, and mirin. Simmer 5 minutes so it comes together.
Boil the udon separately according to the packet, usually 1 to 3 minutes for frozen. Drain.
Thicken the curry broth with the starch slurry. It should coat the noodles rather than run off them.
Divide the udon between deep bowls and ladle the curry over.
Top with spring onion and a heavy shake of shichimi.
recipes.cooksNote: Thickening matters more here than in curry rice. Thin curry slides straight off udon and pools at the bottom of the bowl.

recipes.title: Japanese Cheesecake
recipes.description: Light, wobbly, and barely sweet. It's a soufflé pretending to be a cheesecake, and it lives or dies on your meringue.
method: Line an 18 cm round tin with baking paper, sides taller than the rim. Wrap the outside in foil if it isn't watertight.
Melt the cream cheese, butter, and milk together over a pan of simmering water until completely smooth. Cool slightly.
Whisk in the yolks one at a time, then sift in the flour and cornstarch and whisk until no lumps remain. Add lemon juice and salt.
Whip the whites, adding the sugar in three additions, to soft peaks. The peak should flop over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks will crack the top.
Fold a third of the meringue into the batter to loosen it, then fold in the rest gently in two goes.
Pour into the tin, tap it once on the bench, and set it in a roasting tray. Pour in hot water to come 3 cm up the sides.
Bake at 160°C for 25 minutes, drop to 140°C for 45 minutes, then turn the oven off and leave the door ajar for 15 minutes before removing. The slow cool-down stops it collapsing.
recipes.cooksNote: Some sinking is normal. Dramatic collapse means the meringue was overwhipped or you pulled it out of a hot oven too fast.

recipes.title: Shabu-Shabu
recipes.description: Thin beef swished through hot kombu broth at the table. It's less a recipe than an arrangement, which is exactly why it's good for guests.

items: 800 g beef sirloin or ribeye, sliced 1.5 mm thin (ask a butcher or buy pre-sliced)
½ napa cabbage, 1 bunch shungiku or spinach, 200 g shiitake, 1 packet enoki, 1 leek, 300 g firm tofu, 200 g udon or shirataki
100 ml soy sauce, 80 ml citrus juice (yuzu, or lemon and orange mixed), 50 ml mirin warmed to burn off the alcohol, 5 g katsuobushi, steeped and strained
4 tbsp sesame paste, 2 tbsp soy, 1 tbsp mirin, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, dashi to loosen

method: Soak the kombu in the water for at least 30 minutes, ideally a few hours. Cold soaking gets more flavour with less bitterness than boiling.
Set the pot on a portable burner at the table. Heat until small bubbles rise around the kombu, then remove it before it boils. Add the sake.
Arrange the meat, vegetables, and tofu on platters.
Whisk both sauces and divide into small dipping bowls.
Start with the firmer vegetables and tofu, which need a few minutes in the broth.
Hold each slice of beef with chopsticks and swish it back and forth for 5 to 10 seconds. It should go from red to pink, not grey.
When the meat is finished, cook the noodles in the now-flavourful broth and drink what's left as soup.
recipes.cooksNote: Skim the foam as you go. Ten seconds with a small ladle keeps the broth clear for the end-of-meal noodles.

recipes.title: Yakitori
recipes.description: Grilled chicken skewers, either salted or glazed with tare. The tare is a sauce you build once and keep forever, dipping each batch of skewers back into it.

items: 800 g chicken thigh, in 3 cm pieces
6 spring onions, cut in 3 cm lengths
Chicken skin, hearts, or livers if you want the full range
4 chicken wings or a handful of bones, roasted

method: For the tare, roast the wings until dark, then simmer everything together for 30 minutes until reduced by about a third. Strain.
Thread the chicken and spring onion alternately, packing pieces tightly. Skin side should face outward on each piece.
Build a charcoal fire and rake the coals into a single layer. You want steady radiant heat, not flames.
Grill the skewers over the coals, turning every 45 seconds, for about 4 minutes.
For salt skewers, season before grilling and finish with sansho.
For tare skewers, wait until the chicken is nearly done, then dip into the tare and return to the grill. Repeat three times, letting the glaze set each time.
Serve immediately. Yakitori does not survive a plate journey.
recipes.cooksNote: Dipping before the chicken is cooked burns the sugar and leaves you with bitter, blackened skewers. Glaze at the end only.

recipes.title: Takoyaki
recipes.description: Octopus batter balls from Osaka. They're molten in the centre when done right, which is deliberate, not undercooked.

items: 300 g cooked octopus, in 1.5 cm cubes
Takoyaki sauce, Japanese mayonnaise, aonori, katsuobushi

method: Whisk the flour, eggs, soy, salt, and dashi into a thin batter, about the consistency of single cream. Rest 30 minutes.
Heat a takoyaki pan over medium and oil every well generously, including the flat parts between them.
Fill the wells until the batter overflows across the whole surface. Overfilling is correct here.
Drop a piece of octopus into each well, then scatter spring onion, tenkasu, and ginger across everything.
After 2 minutes the edges will set. Use a skewer to cut the batter between the wells, then turn each ball 90 degrees, tucking the loose batter underneath.
Keep turning every minute or so for about 6 minutes total until they're round and browned all over.
Pile into a tray, zigzag sauce and mayo over the top, then aonori and katsuobushi. The flakes will move in the heat.
recipes.cooksNote: First few balls will be ugly. That's universal. Keep going and the technique clicks around number ten.

recipes.title: Hiroshima-Style Okonomiyaki
recipes.description: Layered rather than mixed, with noodles built into it. Bigger and more of an engineering exercise than the Osaka version.

items: 2 portions yakisoba or ramen noodles, cooked
Okonomiyaki sauce, Japanese mayonnaise, aonori, katsuobushi

method: Whisk the flour and dashi into a thin batter, no thicker than crêpe batter.
Heat a large flat griddle or non-stick pan over medium. Ladle in enough batter to make a 20 cm thin crêpe.
Pile the cabbage on top, mounded high. It looks like far too much. It isn't. Add sprouts, tenkasu, and spring onion.
Lay the pork slices over the pile, then drizzle a little batter over the pork to bind everything.
After 4 minutes, flip the whole stack with two spatulas in one committed motion. Press down gently and cook 6 minutes covered so the cabbage steams down.
On a clear section of the griddle, fry the noodles with a spoonful of sauce, shape them into a disc, then slide the cabbage stack on top.
Fry the eggs flat in another spot, slide the whole tower onto them, flip once more, then sauce, mayo, aonori, katsuobushi.
recipes.cooksNote: The flip is the scary part. Use two wide spatulas, commit fully, and accept that a bit of cabbage will escape. Push it back in.

recipes.title: Hamamatsu Gyoza
recipes.description: Hamamatsu fries its gyoza in a circle and serves them with a pile of boiled bean sprouts in the middle, which cuts the richness. More cabbage than pork in the filling, too.

items: 400 g cabbage, finely chopped, salted and squeezed dry
3 garlic cloves and 2 cm ginger, grated
1 tsp sugar, ½ tsp white pepper
Oil, water, and 1 tsp flour for the crust
Equal soy and rice vinegar, chilli oil, a little grated garlic

method: Salt the chopped cabbage, wait 15 minutes, then wring it out in a cloth. You'll be surprised how much water comes out. Wet filling makes gyoza burst.
Mix the cabbage with pork, onion, garlic, ginger, and seasonings. Stir in one direction until it turns tacky.
Place a teaspoon of filling on each wrapper, wet the edge, and pleat one side against the flat other side.
Heat oil in a non-stick pan. Arrange the gyoza in a spiral, packed close, and fry 2 minutes until the bottoms are golden.
Mix 100 ml water with the teaspoon of flour and pour it in. Cover immediately and steam 6 minutes.
Uncover and let the water cook off entirely. Another 2 minutes gives you a thin lacy crust joining them.
Invert onto a plate so the crisp side faces up, and heap the bean sprouts in the centre.
recipes.cooksNote: The flour-water slurry is what creates that crisp webbing between dumplings. Plain water just steams them.

recipes.title: Unagi (Kabayaki)
recipes.description: Grilled eel lacquered with sweet soy glaze, served over rice as unadon. Fresh eel needs butchering skill most of us don't have, so pre-prepared frozen fillets are the sensible route.

items: 2 prepared unagi fillets, about 200 g each
Eel bones or a piece of kombu, optional
Hot short-grain rice, sansho pepper, pickled ginger

method: Simmer the tare ingredients until reduced by a third and syrupy enough to coat a spoon, about 12 minutes. Set aside.
If your eel came pre-glazed, rinse the sauce off under hot water and pat dry. The packet glaze is usually too sweet.
Steam the fillets for 8 minutes. This is the Kanto method and it makes the flesh noticeably softer.
Sprinkle with sake and grill skin side down under a hot broiler for 3 minutes.
Brush with tare, grill 90 seconds, and repeat twice more. Watch closely, since the sugar catches fast.
Fill bowls with hot rice, spoon a little tare over the rice itself, then lay the eel on top.
Sansho pepper at the table. It's citrusy and slightly numbing, and it cuts the fat.
recipes.cooksNote: Don't skip the sansho. Unagi without it tastes cloying after four or five bites.

recipes.title: Mochi (Daifuku)
recipes.description: Pounded glutinous rice cake wrapped around sweet bean paste. The microwave method takes ten minutes and works genuinely well.

items: 200 g shiratamako or glutinous rice flour
Potato starch or cornstarch for dusting

method: Divide the anko into 10 portions and roll into balls. If using strawberries, wrap each one in anko first and chill.
Whisk the flour, sugar, and water in a microwave-safe bowl until completely smooth.
Cover with cling film and microwave 1 minute. Stir hard with a wet spatula. Microwave 1 minute more, stir again, then 30 seconds. The dough should be translucent, thick, and sticky.
Dust your work surface heavily with starch and tip the hot dough out. Dust the top too.
Let it cool just enough to handle, then divide into 10 pieces.
Flatten each into a disc, place a filling ball in the middle, and gather the edges up and pinch them closed. Roll seam-side down.
Brush off excess starch and eat the same day. Mochi hardens overnight.
recipes.cooksNote: Wet hands and a wet spatula are your only defence against the stickiness. Keep a bowl of water next to you.

recipes.title: Tamagoyaki
recipes.description: Rolled omelette, layer on layer. It looks simple and takes practice. The dashimaki version below has enough dashi in it to be custardy inside.
method: Beat the eggs with everything else. Don't whisk in air. Cut through them with chopsticks instead, then strain through a sieve for a smooth finish.
Heat a rectangular tamagoyaki pan over medium-low. Oil it with a folded paper towel, keeping the towel for reuse between layers.
Pour in a thin layer of egg, tilting to cover the base. Pop any bubbles with your chopsticks.
When the surface is nearly set but still glossy, roll the egg from the far side toward you into a loose log.
Push the roll back to the far end, re-oil the empty pan, and pour in the next layer, lifting the roll so egg runs underneath it.
Repeat until the egg is gone, usually four or five layers.
Turn out onto a bamboo mat, shape gently while warm, then rest 5 minutes and slice into thick pieces.
recipes.cooksNote: Low heat throughout. Browning is considered a fault here, though a pale gold edge is nothing to worry about.

recipes.title: Soba
recipes.description: Buckwheat noodles, served cold with dipping sauce in summer or hot in broth in winter. Making them from scratch is a real skill, so I've written it honestly rather than pretending it's easy.

items: 50 ml mirin, warmed to cook off alcohol
Grated daikon, wasabi, spring onion, shredded nori

method: Mix the flours in a wide bowl. Add water in three stages, mixing with your fingertips in a circular motion so it forms crumbs rather than a lump.
When it holds together when squeezed, gather and knead for 5 minutes into a smooth ball, then cone it and press out the air.
Roll into a large thin sheet, about 1.5 mm, dusting with buckwheat flour as you go. Buckwheat has almost no gluten, so it tears easily. Work gently.
Fold the sheet into layers and cut into 1.5 mm strips with a heavy sharp knife. Toss with flour to keep them separate.
Simmer the tsuyu ingredients briefly, then chill.
Boil the noodles in plenty of unsalted water for 60 to 90 seconds. Fresh soba cooks fast.
Drain and rinse under cold running water, rubbing gently to remove surface starch. Serve on a bamboo tray with the tsuyu and condiments alongside.
recipes.cooksNote: If the dough keeps cracking, raise the white flour to 30 percent. Purists prefer higher buckwheat ratios, but a noodle that holds together beats one that shatters in the pot.

recipes.title: Phanaeng Curry
recipes.description: Thicker and sweeter than red curry, with ground peanuts in the paste and very little liquid. The sauce should cling to the meat rather than pool around it.

items: 10 dried long red chillies, seeded and soaked
1 tsp coriander seed, 1 tsp cumin seed, both toasted
600 g beef sirloin or chicken thigh, sliced thin
400 ml thick coconut milk (don't shake the can)

method: Pound the paste in order: hardest first. Chillies and salt, then lemongrass, galangal, coriander root, lime zest, then shallot and garlic, then the shrimp paste and peanuts. Give it 20 minutes and don't stop until it's smooth.
Spoon the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk into a wok and heat until it splits and the oil rises. This is called cracking the cream.
Fry the paste in that oil for 5 minutes until deeply fragrant and darkened.
Add the meat and stir to coat. Cook 3 minutes.
Add the rest of the coconut milk a little at a time, letting it reduce between additions. You want a thick, glossy sauce, not a soup.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar. It should be salty-sweet with a slow-building heat.
Stir in the shredded lime leaves. Serve topped with whole lime leaves, sliced chilli, basil, and a spoonful of coconut cream.
recipes.cooksNote: Store-bought paste works if you fry it properly and add a tablespoon of ground peanuts, a little extra lemongrass, and lime zest. Frying is what wakes it up.

recipes.title: Tom Kha Gai
recipes.description: Chicken in coconut broth with galangal. Not a chilli-forward soup. It should be sour, creamy, and aromatic, with the heat sitting in the background.

items: 2 stalks lemongrass, bruised and cut in lengths
3 tbsp lime juice, added at the end

method: Simmer the stock with the galangal, lemongrass, lime leaves, shallots, and chillies for 10 minutes so the broth takes on their flavour.
Add the coconut milk and bring back to a gentle simmer. Keep it below a rolling boil from now on.
Add the chicken and poach 6 minutes until just cooked.
Add the mushrooms and cook 3 minutes.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar.
Take the pot off the heat, then stir in the lime juice. Adding it while boiling dulls the flavour and can turn the coconut grainy.
Taste and adjust. Sour first, then salt. Scatter coriander and serve.
recipes.cooksNote: The aromatics stay in the bowl and aren't meant to be eaten. Everyone at a Thai table knows to push them aside.

recipes.title: Phat Kaphrao
recipes.description: Holy basil stir fry with a fried egg on top. The national weeknight dinner. Holy basil, not Thai sweet basil, and if you can't find it, the dish is still good but it's something else.

items: 300 g coarsely chopped pork or chicken (hand-chopped beats minced)

method: Pound the garlic and chillies together into a rough paste. Don't make it smooth.
Heat the wok until it smokes, add oil, then the garlic and chilli. Ten seconds only.
Add the meat and press it flat against the wok to sear before breaking it up. Cook 3 minutes.
Add oyster sauce, fish sauce, dark soy, and sugar. Splash in the stock and let it bubble down into a light sauce.
Kill the heat, throw in the basil, and fold until it just wilts. Any longer and it goes bitter.
In a separate pan, fry the eggs in a shallow pool of hot oil until the whites are blistered and lacy and the yolk is still runny.
Serve over rice with the egg on top and prik nam pla (fish sauce with sliced chilli and lime) on the side.
recipes.cooksNote: Real heat matters more than technique here. If your burner is weak, cook in two smaller batches so the wok doesn't drop temperature and start steaming the meat.

recipes.title: Khao Niao Mamuang
recipes.description: Mango sticky rice. Three components and each one is simple, so any failure is usually the rice. Soak it properly and steam it, never boil.

items: 2 ripe mangoes, Nam Dok Mai or Ataulfo
2 tbsp toasted mung beans or sesame seeds

method: Soak the rice in plenty of cold water for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Skipping this gives you hard centres.
Drain and steam over boiling water, lined with cloth, for 20 to 25 minutes until translucent and tender. Turn it halfway through.
Warm the 300 ml coconut milk with the sugar and salt until dissolved. Don't boil it.
Tip the hot rice into a bowl and pour the sweet coconut milk over. Stir once, then cover and leave 20 minutes.
The rice absorbs all the liquid in that time and turns glossy. Don't panic at how wet it looks initially.
For the topping, whisk the remaining coconut milk with salt and rice flour and heat until slightly thickened.
Slice the mango, plate it beside the rice, spoon the salty coconut sauce over, and scatter the toasted seeds.
recipes.cooksNote: The topping sauce should taste distinctly salty on its own. That contrast against the sweet rice is the point of the dish.

recipes.title: Kai Yang
recipes.description: Grilled marinated chicken from the northeast, served with sticky rice and a tamarind or chilli dipping sauce. Coriander root is the signature flavour and worth hunting down.

items: 6 coriander roots, or 8 stems with leaves stripped
3 tbsp tamarind paste, 2 tbsp fish sauce, 1 tbsp palm sugar, 2 tsp toasted rice powder, 1 tbsp chilli flakes, chopped shallot and coriander

method: Pound the coriander root, garlic, and peppercorns into a paste.
Mix with the fish sauce, oyster sauce, palm sugar, turmeric, coconut milk, and soy.
Rub it into the chicken, getting under the skin, and marinate overnight.
Set up your grill for indirect heat, coals banked to one side.
Cook the chicken skin side up on the cool side, lid down, for 30 minutes.
Move it over the coals for the last 6 to 8 minutes, turning often, to blister the skin. Baste with leftover marinade in the first few minutes only.
Whisk the dipping sauce ingredients together. Rest the chicken 10 minutes, chop through the bone into pieces, and serve with sticky rice and the sauce.
recipes.cooksNote: Toasted rice powder is easy: dry-fry raw glutinous rice with a lime leaf until dark gold, then grind. It gives the sauce its nutty texture.

recipes.title: Pad Thai
recipes.description: Sweet, sour, and salty noodles with tamarind. The version served to tourists is usually sweeter and redder than it should be. Real pad Thai is brown, not orange.

items: 180 g dried flat rice noodles, soaked in warm water 30 minutes
150 g prawns, or firm tofu, or both

method: Dissolve the sauce ingredients together over low heat. Taste it: sour first, then sweet, then salty. Adjust now, because you won't have time later.
Drain the noodles. They should be pliable but still firm.
Heat the wok very hot. Fry the pressed tofu, dried shrimp, and radish for a minute, then the garlic for 10 seconds.
Add the prawns and cook until just pink. Push everything to one side.
Crack the eggs into the empty space, let them set for 20 seconds, then break them up roughly.
Add the noodles and the sauce. Toss constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until the noodles absorb the sauce and turn glossy brown. Add a splash of water if they're still stiff.
Throw in the sprouts and spring onion, toss twice, and serve immediately with peanuts, lime, and chilli flakes.
recipes.cooksNote: Cook two portions maximum at a time. Four portions in one wok drops the heat and you'll get a sticky clump instead of separate noodles.

recipes.title: Khao Phat
recipes.description: Thai fried rice. Cleaner and less sweet than Chinese versions, finished with lime and cucumber. Simple enough that the rice quality shows.

items: 200 g chicken, prawn, or crab meat
Prik nam pla on the side

method: Break up the cold rice with your hands so there are no clumps left.
Heat the wok until smoking. Add oil and the garlic, 10 seconds.
Add the protein and onion, stir-fry 2 minutes.
Push aside, scramble the eggs in the space until just set.
Add the rice and toss hard, using the spatula to press and separate rather than stir gently.
Season with fish sauce, soy, sugar, and pepper. Keep tossing 2 minutes so the rice picks up wok heat.
Add tomato and spring onion at the very end. Plate with cucumber, lime, and coriander, and squeeze the lime over just before eating.
recipes.cooksNote: The lime isn't decoration. Squeezed over at the table it lifts the whole plate, and the dish tastes flat without it.

recipes.title: Pla Thot
recipes.description: Whole fried fish, crisp all the way through, served with a sweet chilli or three-flavour sauce. Scoring and drying are what get you the crunch.

items: 1 whole sea bass, snapper, or tilapia, 800 g, cleaned and scaled
6 garlic cloves, 6 red chillies, 3 coriander roots, pounded

method: Score the fish diagonally to the bone, three or four cuts each side.
Rub with salt inside and out and leave 15 minutes, then pat completely dry with paper towels. Any water left on the skin will spit and stop it crisping.
Dust lightly with rice flour, including inside the cuts.
Heat oil in a wide deep pan to 180°C. There should be enough to come halfway up the fish.
Fry 7 minutes, spooning oil over the exposed side, then turn carefully and fry 6 minutes more. Drain on a rack.
For the sauce, fry the pounded paste in oil for 2 minutes, then add tamarind, sugar, fish sauce, and water. Simmer until syrupy.
Pour the sauce over the fish and scatter with fried garlic, coriander, and sliced chilli.
recipes.cooksNote: A fish spatula and a second person make turning it much less nerve-wracking. If it sticks, it isn't ready to turn.

recipes.title: Khao Op Sapparot
recipes.description: Pineapple fried rice baked in the hollowed-out pineapple. Slightly theatrical, and the baking step genuinely changes the flavour rather than being decoration.
method: Cut the pineapple lengthwise, leaving the leaves on one half. Hollow out the flesh with a knife and spoon, leaving a 1 cm shell.
Dice 250 g of the flesh and set aside. Save the rest for something else.
Heat oil, fry the garlic and onion 2 minutes, then the chicken and prawns until just cooked.
Push aside, scramble the eggs, then add the rice and break it up.
Season with curry powder, turmeric, fish sauce, soy, and sugar. Toss over high heat 3 minutes.
Fold in the diced pineapple, raisins, and half the cashews. Cook 1 minute more so the pineapple doesn't turn to mush.
Pack into the pineapple shell, cover loosely with foil, and bake at 180°C for 20 minutes. Finish with the rest of the cashews, spring onion, and coriander.
recipes.cooksNote: Don't put the pineapple straight on a metal oven rack. Sit it in a baking dish, since the juices will run out of the bottom.

recipes.title: Tod Man Pla
recipes.description: Thai fish cakes, bouncy rather than soft, studded with snake beans and lime leaf. That springy texture comes from working the paste hard.

items: 500 g white fish fillet, cold, roughly chopped
80 g snake beans or green beans, sliced very thin
1 cucumber, 3 shallots, 2 red chillies, all sliced
80 ml rice vinegar, 60 g sugar, ½ tsp salt, 2 tbsp crushed peanuts

method: Blend the fish with the curry paste, egg, fish sauce, sugar, and flour until it forms a sticky paste.
Take it out and slap it against the side of the bowl repeatedly for 3 to 5 minutes. This is what makes it bouncy instead of crumbly.
Fold in the beans and lime leaves by hand.
Chill 20 minutes, then shape into flat discs about 1.5 cm thick with wet hands.
Boil the vinegar, sugar, and salt for the relish, cool, then pour over the cucumber, shallot, and chilli. Add peanuts just before serving.
Heat 2 cm of oil to 170°C. Fry the cakes in batches for 2 to 3 minutes a side until golden and firm.
Drain on a rack and serve hot with the relish.
recipes.cooksNote: Fry one test cake first. If it falls apart, add another tablespoon of rice flour. If it's dense, you overworked it slightly, which is a much smaller problem.

recipes.title: Khanom Chan
recipes.description: Nine steamed layers of coconut and pandan pudding, peeled apart one layer at a time. It takes patience and almost no skill.

items: 60 ml pandan extract (blend 10 pandan leaves with water and strain)

method: Dissolve the sugar in the coconut milk, water, and salt over low heat. Cool completely.
Whisk in the three starches until completely smooth, then strain through a fine sieve.
Divide the batter in half. Colour one half with the pandan extract, adjusting the other half with the same volume of water so the two batters are equally thick.
Steam an oiled 20 cm square tin, empty, for 5 minutes so it's hot.
Pour in a thin layer of green batter, about 4 mm. Steam 5 minutes with a cloth under the lid to catch drips.
Pour a layer of white batter over the set green. Steam 5 minutes. Repeat, alternating, for nine layers, finishing with green.
Steam the final layer 10 minutes. Cool completely, at least 3 hours, before cutting with an oiled knife.
recipes.cooksNote: Each layer must be fully set before the next goes on, or they merge. If in doubt, give it an extra minute.

recipes.title: Kuai-Tiao Ruea
recipes.description: Boat noodles. The broth is dark, heavily spiced, and traditionally thickened with pig's blood, which gives it body and a mineral depth. It's served in small bowls because it's intense.

items: 800 g beef shin and 300 g beef bones
5 star anise, 2 cinnamon sticks, 1 tsp coriander seed, 4 cloves, tied in cloth
Morning glory, bean sprouts, coriander, fried pork rind, chilli vinegar

method: Blanch the bones, drain, and rinse. Simmer with the water, spice bag, garlic, and coriander root for 90 minutes.
Add the beef shin and cook another 45 minutes until tender. Slice it.
Season the broth with both soy sauces, fish sauce, palm sugar, and pickled garlic liquid. It should taste strong, since the noodles will dilute it.
If using blood, whisk it with a ladle of hot broth first, then stir it back into the pot off the boil. Never let it boil after this or it curdles.
Blanch the noodles and morning glory for 20 seconds each.
Build small bowls: noodles, greens, sliced beef, beef balls.
Ladle the hot broth over and top with coriander, pork rind, and chilli vinegar. Two bowls per person is normal.
recipes.cooksNote: Without the blood it's still a good spiced beef noodle soup, just thinner. Add a spoonful of ground toasted rice for a little body instead.

recipes.title: Khao Kha Mu
recipes.description: Pork leg braised in soy and five spice until it collapses, served over rice with pickled greens, boiled egg, and a sharp chilli-garlic sauce.

items: 1 whole pork hock or leg, about 2 kg, skin on
4 star anise, 2 cinnamon sticks, 1 tbsp five spice
Pickled mustard greens, coriander, steamed rice
8 bird's eye chillies, 6 garlic cloves, 3 tbsp vinegar, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tsp salt, blended

method: Scrape and shave the pork skin clean. Blanch the whole hock in boiling water for 10 minutes, then rinse.
Caramelise the palm sugar in a large pot until it turns amber and smells slightly bitter.
Add the water carefully, then both soy sauces, spices, garlic, ginger, and oyster sauce.
Lower the pork in and simmer, covered, for 2½ to 3 hours. Turn it every 40 minutes so the colour is even.
Add the peeled boiled eggs for the last 30 minutes.
The pork is ready when the skin is gelatinous and a chopstick goes through the meat without effort.
Blend the chilli sauce. Chop the pork, pile it over rice, ladle braising liquid over, and add an egg, pickled greens, and plenty of the sharp sauce.
recipes.cooksNote: Chill the braising liquid overnight and lift off the solid fat. You'll want to keep the liquid, since it improves every time you reuse it.

recipes.title: Khanom Fak Bua
recipes.description: Small fried rice-flour cakes that puff up with a raised rim, named for their resemblance to a lotus seed pod. Crisp at the edge, chewy in the middle, and quite obscure even in Thailand.
method: Melt the palm sugar in the water over low heat, then cool.
Whisk the rice flour, tapioca starch, and salt with the coconut milk and sugar syrup into a smooth thick batter.
Rest at room temperature for an hour. It should end up like thick pancake batter, coating a spoon heavily.
Stir in the baking powder and sesame seeds just before frying.
Heat 2 cm of oil to about 165°C in a small deep pan.
Drop in a heaped tablespoon of batter. It sinks, then rises with a puffed ring around the edge. Spoon hot oil over the top as it cooks.
Fry about 3 minutes total until golden and the rim is set. Drain on a rack and eat warm.
recipes.cooksNote: Oil temperature decides the shape. Too cool and it spreads flat, too hot and it browns before the rim can lift.

recipes.title: Som Tam Khai Khem
recipes.description: Green papaya salad with salted duck egg. The salted egg makes it richer and less brutal than the standard version, and the yolk breaks down into the dressing.

items: 300 g green papaya, peeled and shredded into long strands
2 salted duck eggs, boiled 10 minutes, peeled and halved
10 snake beans, cut in 3 cm lengths

method: Soak the shredded papaya in ice water for 15 minutes, then drain hard. It goes crisp and loses any raw taste.
Pound the garlic and chillies in a clay or wooden mortar until broken but not pasty.
Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, lime juice, and tamarind. Pound and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the snake beans and bruise them lightly, then the dried shrimp and peanuts, giving each a few knocks.
Add the tomatoes and press just until they release juice.
Add the papaya. Now switch technique: pound with one hand while turning and lifting with a spoon in the other, so the strands bruise and soak up dressing without turning to pulp.
Taste and adjust, then plate with the salted egg halves on top. Break the yolks into the salad as you eat.
recipes.cooksNote: A granite mortar is too heavy-handed for this. Clay with a wooden pestle is the right tool, because som tam wants bruising rather than crushing.

recipes.title: Soto Betawi
recipes.description: Jakarta's beef soup, made rich with coconut milk and, traditionally, fresh cow's milk. The dairy is what separates it from every other soto in the country. It's heavy in the best way.

items: 800 g beef brisket or shin, in 3 cm cubes
300 g beef tripe or lung, optional but traditional
2 tsp salt, plus more to taste
Fried shallots, diced tomato, spring onion, emping crackers, lime wedges, sambal

method: Cover the beef with the water, bring to a boil, and skim the grey foam off the top for the first ten minutes. Skimming properly is what gives you a clear-tasting broth.
Add lemongrass, lime leaves, salam, galangal, cinnamon, and cloves. Simmer gently, lid ajar, for about 90 minutes until the beef is tender.
Meanwhile blend the paste ingredients into a smooth purée with a splash of water. Fry in the oil over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the oil separates.
Scrape the fried paste into the pot. Simmer 20 minutes more.
Stir in the coconut milk and fresh milk. Keep the heat low from here. Boiling hard will split it.
Season with salt. Taste. It should be savoury and slightly sweet, never spicy on its own.
Ladle over the garnishes in each bowl and serve with white rice and sambal on the side.
recipes.cooksNote: If tripe makes you nervous, boil it separately with a slice of ginger for 45 minutes first, then drain and add it to the pot. That handles the smell.

recipes.title: Bakso
recipes.description: Indonesian meatball soup. The texture is the whole point: bouncy, almost springy, nothing like an Italian meatball. You get there with very cold meat, ice, and a lot of blending.

items: 500 g beef topside, trimmed of sinew, cut in cubes and frozen 30 minutes
1.5 litres beef stock or bone broth
4 garlic cloves, fried whole then crushed
Yellow noodles, rice vermicelli, blanched bok choy, celery leaves, fried shallots, sambal, sweet soy sauce

method: Blend the half-frozen beef with garlic, salt, pepper, and the ice until it becomes a smooth, pale, sticky paste. Work in batches so the machine doesn't heat up.
Add the tapioca starch, baking powder, and egg white. Blend just until combined.
Chill the mixture 20 minutes. Bring a wide pot of water to a bare simmer, around 80°C.
Squeeze the paste between your thumb and forefinger to form balls, scooping each one off with an oiled spoon straight into the water.
They sink first, then float. Once they float, give them two more minutes, then lift out.
Heat the stock with the crushed fried garlic and pepper. Season well.
Build each bowl with noodles, greens, meatballs, then hot broth. Garnish at the table.
recipes.cooksNote: If your meatballs come out crumbly, the mix got warm. Everything should stay near freezing until it hits the water.

recipes.title: Coto Makassar
recipes.description: From South Sulawesi, and unlike most Indonesian soups it's thickened with ground peanuts and toasted rice rather than coconut milk. Traditionally it uses every part of the cow. You can keep it to brisket and nobody will arrest you.

items: 1 kg beef brisket, plus offal if you want it
2.5 litres water, ideally including rice washing water
100 g raw peanuts, fried and ground
3 tbsp raw rice, toasted dry until golden, then ground
Fried shallots, spring onion, lime, tauco or fermented soybean sambal, ketupat rice cakes

method: Boil the beef in the water with salam, galangal, and lemongrass until tender, about 2 hours. Skim as it comes up to the boil.
Lift out the meat, slice it, and keep the broth. Strain it if you want it neater.
Blend the paste, then fry it in oil for 7 minutes until fragrant and the oil separates.
Stir the ground peanuts and ground toasted rice into the paste, then add a ladle of broth to loosen it.
Pour the whole lot back into the broth pot. Simmer 30 minutes so it thickens and the flavours settle.
Return the sliced beef. Season with salt.
Serve with the sambal tauco stirred in to taste. That fermented hit is what makes it Makassar.
recipes.cooksNote: Cooking the beef in the cloudy water left over from rinsing rice is a real technique here, not superstition. It softens the meat and adds body.

recipes.title: Nasi Goreng Jawa
recipes.description: Javanese fried rice, distinguished from the more common version by sweet soy sauce and a pounded chilli paste with shrimp paste in it. Darker, sweeter, and better.

items: 3 cups cold cooked rice, at least a day old
Handful of shredded cabbage and sliced mustard greens
5 red bird's eye chillies, more if you like
Fried egg, prawn crackers, sliced cucumber and tomato, fried shallots

method: Pound or blend the shallots, garlic, chillies, and terasi to a rough paste.
Heat the oil in a wok over high heat. Fry the paste 3 minutes until it darkens.
Push it aside, crack in the eggs, and scramble them roughly in the same pan.
Add the chicken. Cook until it's no longer pink.
Toss in the cabbage and greens for 30 seconds, then the rice. Break up every clump with the back of your spatula.
Pour the kecap manis around the edge of the wok, not into the middle. It caramelises on the hot metal on the way in.
Season, toss hard for 2 minutes, finish with spring onion, and get it onto plates while it's still steaming.
recipes.cooksNote: Day-old rice is not optional. Fresh rice steams instead of frying and you end up with porridge.

recipes.title: Nasi Padang (Rendang and Sambal Ijo)
recipes.description: Nasi Padang is a spread, not a single dish: rice with a crowd of Minangkabau side dishes. Here are the two that anchor any table. Rendang takes four hours and rewards every one of them.

items: 1.2 kg beef chuck, in large 4 cm cubes
1.5 litres coconut milk (thick, from about 3 fresh coconuts or 4 cans)
3 turmeric leaves if you can find them
250 g green bird's eye and long green chillies
4 tbsp oil, salt, squeeze of lime

method: Blend the rendang paste until completely smooth. Lumpy paste means lumpy sauce.
Put the paste, coconut milk, aromatics, and beef into a wide heavy pot. Do not cover it.
Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Stir every 15 minutes or so at first.
After about 2 hours the liquid turns pale gold and thickens. This stage is kalio, and some people stop here. It's good, but keep going.
Over the next 90 minutes to 2 hours the coconut oil separates out and the sauce goes from creamy to dark brown to almost dry. Stir constantly through this last stretch or it will catch.
It's done when the meat is coated in dark, oily, almost crumbly paste and there's no free liquid. Season.
For the sambal ijo, steam or boil the chillies, tomatoes, shallots, and garlic for 5 minutes, then pound coarsely and stir-fry in oil for 5 minutes. Salt, lime, done.
Serve both with plenty of rice, plus whatever else you feel like adding.
recipes.cooksNote: Widen the pot, don't deepen it. Evaporation is doing the work, and a narrow pot takes twice as long.

recipes.title: Rawon
recipes.description: East Javanese black beef soup. The colour comes from keluak, a fermented nut that tastes faintly of truffle and dark chocolate. Nothing else does what it does.

items: 800 g beef shin or brisket, cubed
Salt and a little palm sugar
Short bean sprouts, salted duck egg, fried shallots, sambal terasi, lime

method: Crack the keluak shells, scoop out the black paste, and soak it in warm water for 15 minutes. Discard any that smell sharp or bitter rather than earthy.
Boil the beef in the water until tender, roughly 90 minutes, skimming early.
Blend the spice paste with the soaked keluak until smooth.
Fry the paste in oil with the lemongrass, lime leaves, salam, and galangal for 8 minutes.
Tip it into the broth. Simmer 30 minutes so the colour and flavour spread through.
Season with salt and a pinch of palm sugar to round it off.
Serve over rice with raw bean sprouts on top. The crunch against the dark broth is the best part.
recipes.cooksNote: Buy keluak already cracked and cleaned if your shop sells it that way. The whole nuts are genuinely hard to open without a hammer.

recipes.title: Gado Gado
recipes.description: Blanched vegetables under peanut sauce. The sauce is where all the attention goes, and it should be thick enough to coat but loose enough to pour.

items: 250 g raw peanuts, fried in oil until golden, then cooled
300 ml hot water, more as needed
200 g green beans, cut in lengths
200 g firm tofu and 150 g tempeh, both fried

method: Grind the fried peanuts with the chillies, garlic, and terasi. A mortar gives better texture than a blender, but use what you have.
Add palm sugar, tamarind, and salt. Grind again.
Loosen with hot water a splash at a time until it pours slowly off a spoon. Taste and balance: it wants to be nutty, sweet, sour, and salty all at once.
Blanch each vegetable separately in salted water. Beans need 3 minutes, cabbage 2, spinach and sprouts about 30 seconds. Drain well.
Arrange everything on a platter with the tofu, tempeh, potato, egg, and cucumber.
Pour the sauce over just before serving, or serve it alongside so nothing goes soggy.
Finish with crackers and fried shallots.
recipes.cooksNote: Frying raw peanuts yourself beats using roasted ones from a jar by a wide margin. Cool them completely before grinding or the sauce turns oily.

recipes.title: Pempek Palembang
recipes.description: Fish and sago cakes served in a sour, sweet, garlicky vinegar sauce called cuko. The sauce is aggressive and it should be.

items: 500 g Spanish mackerel fillet, skinned and boned, minced
4 eggs, for the stuffed kapal selam version

method: Mix the minced fish with the ice water, salt, sugar, and garlic until it looks like a smooth wet paste.
Fold in the flour gradually with your hands. Stop as soon as it holds together. Kneading it develops toughness.
For kapal selam, shape a portion into a thick cup, drop in a whole raw egg, and seal the edges carefully.
Simmer the shaped pempek in salted water until they float, then 5 minutes more. Lift out and cool.

For the cuko, boil the palm sugar with the water until dissolved. Pound the garlic and chillies, add them with the tamarind and dried shrimp, and simmer 15 minutes. Strain if you like it smooth. Add vinegar and salt off the heat.
Deep fry the boiled pempek in hot oil until the outside blisters and turns golden.
Cut into pieces, drown in cuko, and top with diced cucumber and yellow noodles.
recipes.cooksNote: Boiled pempek keeps in the fridge for three days and freezes for a month. Fry it fresh each time.

recipes.title: Batagor
recipes.description: Bandung street food: fried fish dumplings and tofu under peanut sauce. The name is a contraction of bakso tahu goreng, which tells you exactly what's in it.

items: 300 g mackerel or tenggiri fillet, minced
1 tsp salt, ½ tsp white pepper, ½ tsp sugar
6 squares firm tofu, halved into pockets

method: Combine the fish, prawn, flour, egg, garlic, spring onion, and seasoning into a sticky paste.
Hollow out each tofu square slightly and pack it with filling.
Push a spoonful of filling into each wonton wrapper, gathering the edges up loosely so it looks like a little sack.
Heat the oil to 170°C. Fry the tofu and dumplings in batches for 5 to 6 minutes until deep golden and firm.
Grind the sauce ingredients together, then thin with hot water to a pourable consistency. Season.
Cut everything into bite-sized pieces on the plate.
Spoon over the sauce, then add sweet soy sauce, lime, and sambal.
recipes.cooksNote: Fry at a moderate temperature. Too hot and the wrapper browns before the fish paste inside is cooked through.

recipes.title: Martabak Manis
recipes.description: A thick sweet pancake, sliced, buttered heavily, and stuffed. Called terang bulan in some cities. The holes in the surface are the mark of a good one, and they come from resting the batter properly.

items: Grated chocolate, crushed roasted peanuts, cheddar, sesame seeds, whatever you like

method: Whisk the flour, sugar, salt, and yeast together. Beat in the eggs and half the liquid until smooth, then add the rest.
Cover and rest at room temperature for an hour. The batter should look bubbly on top.
Stir in the baking soda right before cooking. This is what makes the holes open up.
Heat a heavy, deep, non-stick pan over medium-low. Pour in enough batter to fill it about 2 cm deep.
Cook undisturbed. Holes will appear across the surface over 4 or 5 minutes. Once they've formed and the surface looks dry at the edges, sprinkle a spoonful of sugar over the top.
Cover and cook another 5 minutes until the centre is set.
Turn out, brush the entire surface generously with butter, add fillings and condensed milk, fold in half, and slice.
recipes.cooksNote: Low heat throughout. High heat gives you a burnt base and a raw middle, which is the classic failure here.

recipes.title: Nasi Uduk
recipes.description: Rice cooked in coconut milk with lemongrass and pandan. Jakarta breakfast food. It's simple enough that quality depends entirely on the coconut milk you use.

items: 400 g jasmine rice, rinsed until the water runs nearly clear
Fried chicken, omelette strips, tempe orek, fried shallots, sambal kacang, cucumber

method: Warm the coconut milk, water, aromatics, salt, and coriander in a pot. Don't let it boil hard.
Add the rinsed rice. Cook over medium heat, stirring now and then, until the liquid is absorbed and the rice looks pitted with steam holes.
Tip the rice into a steamer lined with cloth or banana leaf, aromatics and all.
Steam for 20 to 25 minutes until each grain is tender and separate.
Fluff with a fork, pull out the lemongrass and leaves, and let it sit uncovered for a minute.
Pile onto plates with the sides and a good spoonful of sambal.
recipes.cooksNote: The two-stage absorb-then-steam method is worth the extra pot. Cooking it entirely in a rice cooker gives you a stickier, heavier result.

recipes.title: Bebek Goreng Madura
recipes.description: Duck simmered in spices until tender, then deep fried hard. Served with sambal pencit or the fierce green sambal Madura is known for.

items: 1 whole duck, about 1.8 kg, cut into 4 or 8 pieces
4 salam leaves, 3 lemongrass stalks, 5 cm galangal
1 tsp terasi, salt, lime, 3 tbsp hot oil

method: Rub the duck all over with salt and lime juice, leave 10 minutes, then rinse. This cuts the gaminess.
Blend the paste and fry it in a large pot with a little oil for 8 minutes.
Add the duck, aromatics, and water. Simmer, partly covered, for about 75 minutes until a fork slides into the thigh with no resistance.
Let the duck cool in the liquid if you have time. It'll take on more flavour.
Lift out and pat completely dry. Wet duck spits violently in hot oil.
Deep fry at 180°C for 5 to 7 minutes until the skin is dark and crisp.
Pound the sambal ingredients coarsely, then pour the hot oil over the top and stir. Serve with rice.
recipes.cooksNote: Save the simmering liquid. Reduced down and spooned over rice, it's better than most gravies.

recipes.title: Sate Ayam Ponorogo
recipes.description: Ponorogo satay uses long strips of chicken breast rather than cubes, marinated before grilling, which gives you more surface for char. The peanut sauce is thinner than the Madura version.

items: 700 g chicken breast, sliced into long thin strips
4 tbsp kecap manis mixed with 2 tbsp oil and a squeeze of lime

method: Toss the chicken strips with the marinade. Cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours.
Thread each strip lengthwise onto a skewer, weaving it so it lies flat.
Grind the peanuts with the fried shallots, garlic, and chillies, then simmer with the rest of the sauce ingredients for 10 minutes until it thickens slightly.
Get your coals properly hot and let the flames die down to glowing embers.
Grill the skewers 2 minutes a side, basting each time you turn them.
Watch the sugar. It goes from caramelised to burnt fast, so move skewers to cooler spots as needed.
Serve with sauce, sliced shallot, lime, and either rice or lontong.
recipes.cooksNote: A gas grill or a hot ridged pan works, but you lose the smoke, which is a real part of the flavour. Compensate with an extra minute over higher heat.

recipes.title: Sate Kambing
recipes.description: Goat satay. Cubes of leg or shoulder, often with a piece of fat between them, grilled fast and served with sweet soy, raw shallot, and chilli rather than peanut sauce.

items: 800 g young goat leg or shoulder, in 2.5 cm cubes
1 ripe papaya, or 2 tbsp grated green papaya

method: Rub the goat with the grated papaya and leave 30 minutes. The enzymes tenderise it. Don't leave it longer than an hour or the surface goes mushy.
Rinse the papaya off, then marinate with kecap manis, garlic, salt, and pepper for another 30 minutes.
Thread 4 or 5 cubes per skewer, packed close together so they stay juicy.
Grill over very hot coals. Two minutes a side, no more. Goat toughens the moment it overcooks.
Mix the shallots, chillies, tomato, and kecap manis in a bowl.
Slide the meat off the skewers onto that mixture, or serve them alongside.
Squeeze lime over and eat immediately.
recipes.cooksNote: Young goat has a mild flavour. If yours smells strong, soak the cubes in milk for an hour before you do anything else.

recipes.title: Pecel Lele
recipes.description: Fried catfish with sambal and raw vegetables. It's the default cheap dinner on Java, sold from tarpaulin stalls every night. The sambal does most of the work.

items: 4 catfish, about 250 g each, cleaned and scored
Cucumber, cabbage leaves, Thai basil, long beans, rice

method: Rub the fish inside and out with garlic, turmeric, salt, and lime. Rest 15 minutes.
Fry the sambal ingredients (except sugar and salt) in the oil over medium heat for 6 minutes until softened and blistered.
Pound or blend them coarsely with the sugar and salt. Leave it rough. Smooth sambal loses something.
Heat the frying oil to 180°C in a deep pan.
Pat the fish dry and lower it in carefully. Fry 6 to 8 minutes until the skin is dark and crunchy at the edges.
Drain on a rack, not paper, so the underside stays crisp.
Serve on a plate with the sambal, the raw vegetables, and hot rice. Tear the fish apart with your hands and drag it through the sambal.
recipes.cooksNote: Score the fish down to the bone on both sides. It cooks faster and gets crisp in the cuts, which is where the best bites are.
